summary: The paper extends the error generator formalism to mid-circuit measurements (MCMs) on superconducting qubits by modeling MCM errors using a circuit gadget representation and decomposing quantum instruments into physically interpretable elementary deviations. Gate set tomography characterization of a transmon dispersive readout reveals amplitude damping ($T_1$ effects), readout error, imperfect collapse (weakness), and AC Stark shift-induced non-Markovianity, with errors quantified as functions of readout pulse amplitude across $V = 0$ to $1.8 \times V_0$.
motivation: Quantum error correction requires high-fidelity MCMs, but their errors are difficult to interpret from estimated quantum instruments. While error generators have successfully decomposed gate errors into physical mechanisms, no analogous framework existed for MCMs, limiting diagnostic capabilities for measurement debugging and mitigation.
method: The authors adapted error generators to MCMs by constructing a two-qubit gadget (CNOT with virtual qubit) that represents an MCM, enabling the extraction of 28 first-order MCM-gauge-invariant (FOMGI) quantities via gate set tomography on a transmon with $\chi_{01}/2\pi = -0.26$ MHz and $\kappa/2\pi = 0.16$ MHz, swept across readout amplitudes with $N = 8 \times 10^3$ to $4 \times 10^4$ shots per circuit.
result: Pre-MCM amplitude damping increases with readout amplitude while post-MCM decay remains constant, pure readout error and weakness dominate below $V = 0.6 \times V_0$, and a measure-and-prepare model with one additional AC Stark shift parameter achieves $N_\sigma < 2$ model violation at the nominal amplitude, reducing required parameters from 28 to 43 without sacrificing predictive accuracy.
